paragraphs: Baker, here's the big idea: death is not the end of the story, and what God raises is far better than what goes into the ground. Paul says a seed doesn't look like the plant it becomes, and God gives each one the body He designed (1 Corinthians 15:37-38). So the body that is sown is perishable, and it is raised imperishable. It is sown in weakness and raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42-43). I sat in a drawer with my edges worn soft, so I like hearing that weakness is not the last word!

Now for the part that makes my mustache twirl. Paul says flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, so we need to be changed (1 Corinthians 15:50-51). We have borne the likeness of the earthly man, and we shall bear the likeness of the heavenly man (1 Corinthians 15:49). Death looks big, baker, but Paul talks right to it and says, "Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:55). The sting of death is sin, and that's why the victory is a gift: "But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!" (1 Corinthians 15:56-57).

So what do you do with a victory that's already yours? Paul says, "be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58). That means the small, quiet work you do for the Lord counts, even on the days nobody sees it. It's why my ovens stay ready, and I don't need to know the day to keep them warm. Keep your apron on, friend, because your labor in the Lord is not in vain!
